paragraphs: On every weekday a person completes a hundred berachot through the morning blessings and the blessings of the prayer service from beginning to end, and through the blessings over eating and drinking. On Shabbat and Yom Tov, where the blessings of the Amidah are fewer, one completes the count with [blessings over] various fruits and spices. On a fast day, many blessings are lacking, especially when fasting a full night and day without eating or drinking at all; one should take care to listen to the blessings of those called up to the Torah and answer Amen after them, and this helps to complete the count in a time of difficulty when there is no other way — but one must hear the entire blessing from beginning to end.

clarification.explanation: On every weekday a person completes a hundred berachot through the morning blessings, the blessings of the prayer service from its beginning to its end, and the blessings over eating and drinking. On Shabbat and Yom Tov, where blessings are lacking from the (shortened) Amidah prayer, one completes the count with [blessings over] various fruits and spices. On a fast day — especially a fast lasting a full night and day without eating or drinking — many blessings are lacking, and so it is fitting to listen to the blessings of those called up to the Torah and answer Amen, which helps complete the count in a time of difficulty; but one must hear the entire blessing from beginning to end.
takeaways: Every day one completes a hundred berachot (on Shabbat/Yom Tov — with blessings over fruits and spices).
On a fast day, listening to the Torah-reading blessings and answering Amen helps complete the count.

paragraphs: One who recites a berachah must make it audible to his own ears, and must take care to bless slowly and with intention of the heart, unlike those unlearned people who bless while skipping letters and words. And if he skipped [God's] Name or [His] Kingship, he must go back and recite the berachah again, for any berachah lacking Name and Kingship is not a berachah at all. And even if he skipped only the word 'ha'olam' (the world/universe) alone, he must go back and bless again, for 'King' alone is not 'Kingship'.

clarification.explanation: One who recites a berachah must make it audible to his own ears, and must bless slowly and with intention of the heart — not by skipping letters and words as the masses do. If he skipped God's Name or 'Kingship' (King of the world) he must go back and bless again, for a berachah without Name and Kingship is not a berachah at all; and even if he skipped only the word 'ha'olam' (the world), he must go back, because 'King' alone is not 'Kingship'.
takeaways: A berachah must contain God's Name and 'Kingship' (including the word 'ha'olam') in full — any omission requires repeating the berachah.

paragraphs: One must be careful not to pause between the berachah and the eating or drinking for longer than the time it takes to say a short greeting — namely, the time it takes to say 'Shalom alekha Rabbi' ('Peace be upon you, my teacher'), which is three words. A hint to this: 'In the gate he shall not open his mouth' (Proverbs 24:7) — the Hebrew letters of 'ba-sha'ar' (in the gate) are an acronym for 'the measure of Shalom alekha Rabbi.' However, in cutting the bread for 'HaMotzi' when eating with others, it was permitted to cut a large slice in order to give from it to those at the table, and even though cutting a large slice this way takes longer than the permitted pause, this was permitted for the sake of the mitzvah [of hospitality/sharing]. In any case, one should be careful to eat from that very slice before cutting from it for the others at the table. Therefore, if one is about to drink water and wishes to pour out some of it [to avoid overfilling or for another reason], he should pour it out before reciting the berachah, so as to be able to drink promptly after the berachah. There is also another reason not to pour out water after the berachah: the disgrace this shows to the berachah, which has already taken effect on all the water in the vessel, as Rabbeinu Zalman of blessed memory wrote. Likewise one must be careful, when drinking a hot beverage, not to purse his lips to cool it after the berachah, but rather to do so before. And one should be careful not to recite a berachah over an extremely hot food or drink, because of the concern that he may delay [drinking/eating] on account of the heat; see Chesed LaAlafim.

clarification.explanation: One must not pause between the berachah and the eating/drinking for longer than 'the time it takes to speak' (the time needed to say 'Shalom alekha Rabbi' — three words). In cutting the 'HaMotzi' bread when eating with others, it was permitted to cut a large slice in order to give some to those at the table (even though this takes longer than the permitted pause, because it serves a mitzvah), but one should taste from the slice before giving from it to the others. Therefore, one who is about to drink water and wants to pour out some of it should pour it out before the berachah; and likewise one should not purse the lips to cool a hot drink after the berachah, but rather beforehand.
takeaways: One may not pause between the berachah and eating for longer than 'the time it takes to speak' (except for cutting bread for others at the table — permitted, though one should taste it first).
Preparations such as pouring off excess water or cooling a hot drink are done before the berachah, not after.

paragraphs: If his heart can see his nakedness because he has no belt or his garment is not snug, he may not recite a berachah; likewise, with head uncovered, he may not recite a berachah. Whatever he blesses over, he should hold in his right hand. The Sefer Chassidim writes that if a book is handed to him, he must take it in his right hand. One should not skewer the fruit he is blessing over with a knife and hold it in his right hand, for these are two opposites: the right hand is the source from which life comes forth, while the knife shortens [life] — see Eshel Avraham and Rabbeinu Zalman of blessed memory. One must also be careful that the fork be of silver and not of iron, for there are cases where one is compelled to skewer something with a fork in order to recite a berachah over it.

clarification.explanation: One whose nakedness would be visible to his own eye — because he has no belt and no snug-fitting garment — may not recite a berachah, and likewise one with an uncovered head may not recite a berachah. What one blesses over should be held in the right hand. One should not skewer fruit with a knife in order to bless it while holding it in the right hand, since the right hand symbolizes life while the knife shortens life — two opposites; but if a fork is needed, it should be of silver rather than iron.
takeaways: One may not recite a berachah while one's nakedness is exposed or the head is uncovered; hold what is being blessed in the right hand.
Avoid a knife (which shortens) when blessing over fruit; a silver fork is preferable to an iron one.

paragraphs: One who stands by a stream of water recites a berachah and drinks from the stream, even though the water that was before him at the time of the berachah has already flowed past and moved on, because his intent was for the water that would arrive by the time he finished his berachah, and the berachah took effect on that water. Moreover, even if he took a fruit in his hand from a vessel containing fruits and blessed over it, and by the end of the berachah it fell from his hand and was lost or became repulsive, he may take another fruit from the vessel and eat it relying on that same berachah, because his intent was also to eat from the fruits in the vessel [generally], and so the berachah took effect on them as well — even though some disagree in this matter of the fallen fruit, nevertheless since we hold that in a doubt about berachot we are lenient, he should not bless again. This applies specifically when, at the time of the berachah, his intent was to eat further from what was before him even had the fruit not fallen from his hand. The same law applies if he blessed over a cup of wine and it spilled, and there was a jug of wine sitting before him and his intent was to drink more from it. But if his intent was only to eat that specific fruit that was in his hand, and only to drink that specific cup that was in his hand — now that it was lost or spilled, his berachah turns out to have been in vain, and he should say 'Blessed is the Name of His glorious Kingdom forever and ever.' And if he then wishes to eat fruit from the general supply, he must go back and recite the berachah again; however, even here he should try to bring another person to bless over the fruit while he has intent to be included by it, or bring a fruit of another kind whose berachah is the same as that fruit, and bless over it [instead]. All this applies if he had finished the berachah, having said the word 'Eloheinu' as well; but if he had said only 'Barukh atah Hashem' and the fruit or cup fell from his hand [before finishing], he should complete the sentence with 'Lamdeni chukekha' ('teach me Your statutes'), so that it appears as though he is reciting a verse of Psalms [rather than a truncated berachah], and then he may take another fruit and bless over it.

clarification.explanation: One standing beside a water channel who blesses over the water in order to drink — even though the water that was before him at the time of the berachah has already flowed past — may drink from the water that comes afterward, because his intent was on that water. Likewise, if he blessed over a fruit and it fell from his hand before he ate it, he may take another fruit from the same vessel and eat it relying on the berachah, because his intent was to eat from those [fruits generally]. This applies specifically when he intended from the start to eat more from the vessel; but if he intended only that specific fruit/cup and it was lost — his berachah was in vain (he says 'Barukh shem kevod malkhuto le'olam va'ed'), and if he wants to eat more he must bless again (or have someone else bless with intent to include him). All of this applies once he had already said the word 'Eloheinu' in his berachah; but if he had said only 'Barukh atah Hashem' and the fruit or cup fell from his hand before he completed the berachah, he should finish with 'Lamdeni chukekha' (Psalms 119:12), so that it appears as a verse of Psalms rather than an interrupted berachah, and then take another fruit and bless over it.
takeaways: A berachah intended also to cover additional water/fruit from the same source covers them even if the first is lost.
A berachah intended only for one specific item that was lost is in vain, and a new berachah is required (or another person blesses on his behalf).

paragraphs: If he took a fruit in his hand and blessed over it, and then saw another fruit nicer than it, he should not switch to it, even though at the time he recited the berachah his intent was also to include that other fruit.

clarification.explanation: One who took a fruit in hand and blessed over it, and then saw a nicer fruit — should not switch to it, even though at the time of the berachah he had intended to include that other fruit as well.
takeaways: One may not switch to a nicer fruit after already having blessed over the first one, even if he had intended it in advance.

paragraphs: If he was eating fruit casually and more was brought to him: if from the start his intent had been on whatever would be brought to him, he need not go back and bless again on what was brought, even though he had already eaten everything that was before him. But if from the start his intent had been only to eat those specific fruits before him, and he then reconsidered and decided to eat more and asked that more be brought — he must recite a berachah over what is brought, even if some of the [original] fruit is still before him. And if he ate without any specific intent [either way], then as long as some of the fruit he already blessed over remains before him, there is a dispute on this matter: some say he must bless again [on the new fruit], and some say he need not. And since we hold that in a doubt about berachot we are lenient, he should not bless again. However, even though the halachic authorities write that we say 'a doubt about berachot, be lenient' even in a case of 'get up and eat' [i.e., even proactively, not only after the fact] — see Chesed LaAlafim, siman 206, in the addendum, letter heh — nevertheless, wherever it is possible for us to remedy [the doubt] in a 'get up and eat' situation, we do remedy it: namely, he should recite the berachah of 'shehakol' over a bit of sugar, and thereby also discharge the obligation for that fruit; or another person should come and recite the berachah and eat, with intent to include him. And if none of these options is possible, he should recite the berachah without [uttering] God's Name and Kingship, and merely contemplate the Name and Kingship in his heart. All this applies when he ate without specific intent and some of the fruit he had already blessed over remains before him — this is the case of the dispute mentioned above. But if he ate without specific intent and finished everything that was before him, and only afterward more was brought to him — he must bless, according to all opinions, on what was brought, since he was eating casually; and there is no difference whether what was brought is of the same kind or of a different kind whose berachah is the same as the first. And if he had established himself at the table specifically to eat fruit, then even if he finished everything before him and afterward more was brought, he need not bless again, for one who has established himself for eating fruit does not lose his original intent as long as he remains seated at the table; and here too there is no difference between being brought the same kind or a kind whose berachah is the same.

clarification.explanation: One who ate fruit casually (without formally establishing himself for it) and more was brought to him: if from the start his intent had covered also what would be brought, he need not bless again on the addition, even though he had already finished what was before him. If from the start he intended only the fruit before him, and then reconsidered and asked for more — he must bless on what was brought, even if some of the first fruit remains. If he ate with no specific intent either way, then as long as some of the fruit he already blessed over remains before him, there is a dispute: some say he must bless on the addition, some say not; and since a doubt about berachot is resolved leniently, he should not bless. But since the doubt can be remedied, it is preferable: he should bless 'shehakol' over a bit of sugar and thereby discharge the fruit as well, or have another person bless and eat with intent to include him; and if neither is possible, he should bless without uttering God's Name and Kingship, merely contemplating them in his heart. All this dispute applies specifically when he ate without specific intent and some of the first fruit still remains before him. But if he ate without specific intent and finished everything before him, and only then was more brought — he blesses on the addition according to all opinions, since he ate casually; and it makes no difference whether what was brought is the same kind or another kind with the same berachah. And if he had established himself at the table for eating fruit — then even having finished everything before him and having more brought, he does not bless again, since one who has established himself does not lose his intent as long as he remains seated at the table; and here too there is no difference between the same kind and a kind with the same berachah.
takeaways: Intent covering the addition in advance — no new berachah; reconsidering and asking for more — a new berachah is required, even if some of the original remains.
Eating with no specific intent while some of the original fruit remains — doubtful, so no new berachah (best resolved via a 'shehakol' over sugar).
Finishing everything eaten casually and then having more brought — bless according to all opinions; having established oneself for the meal — no new berachah.

paragraphs: Even one who established himself for eating fruit — if he finished eating and the fruit was cleared away from before him, and he resolved in his mind to recite the closing berachah, but did not yet recite the closing berachah because some time passed while he was occupied with something else, and afterward he found, of that same kind of fruit, [a piece] that had fallen onto the bed, or into a corner, or on the floor — this is certainly regarded as having 'reconsidered,' and he must recite a berachah over that fruit he found if he wishes to eat it. However, it is better that he restrain himself from eating it, so as to avoid the berachah altogether.

clarification.explanation: One who established himself for eating fruit, finished, and the fruit was cleared away, and he had resolved to recite the closing berachah but had not yet done so because he became occupied with something else in the meantime — if he then found, of that same kind, [a piece] that had fallen (on the bed, in a corner, or on the floor), this is regarded as having 'reconsidered,' and he must bless if he wants to eat it. It is preferable to refrain from eating it so as to avoid the doubt of a berachah.
takeaways: Fruit found after a fruit-meal has ended (that had fallen earlier) has the status of 'reconsidering' — one blesses over it if he wishes to eat it.

paragraphs: If, after he blessed over what was before him and ate from it, they brought him a fruit of another kind whose berachah is the same, but it is more important and dearer to him than the first kind that was before him — he must recite a berachah over the new one, unless he had explicitly intended to discharge it with the berachah over the first, for it is not proper that a fruit which is not [as] important should discharge a more important, dearer fruit incidentally, unless he specifically intended to discharge it — see Chayei Adam, klal 60, se'if 2. All this applies only to a person eating from his own [food]; but one eating at another's table, once he has blessed over one kind, is discharged for whatever else is brought to him, even if none of the first kind remains before him, since it all depends on the host's intent — unless he has truly reconsidered. And whenever one is eating at the table of a host, even if the host had not originally intended to give the guests more than what was before them, but gave more only at the guests' request — even so, they need not go back and bless again, because they rely on the host's mind, knowing that he will give them all they need, and they do not lose their original intent; see Chayei Adam, klal 60, se'if 5.

clarification.explanation: If, after blessing and eating, another fruit of the same berachah is brought that is more important and dearer to him than the first — he must bless again on it, unless he had explicitly intended to discharge it as well with the first berachah (one does not discharge something important via something less important incidentally). This applies to one eating his own food; but one eating at another's table — his berachah on one kind discharges everything else brought to him, since it all depends on the host's intent (unless he truly reconsidered).
takeaways: A more important fruit brought after the berachah requires a new berachah, unless it was intended in advance.
One eating at a host's table is discharged by whatever is brought, since he relies on the host's intent.

paragraphs: A guest entering his friend's house who is brought a cup of sugar-water whose berachah is 'shehakol,' and afterward is brought coffee whose berachah is also 'shehakol' — he should not bless on the coffee, for it is discharged by the first berachah, because some people honor a guest with coffee alone, and some honor him with both this and that. However, it is good for the guest to have intent, with the first drink brought to him, to discharge also the other drink that will be handed to him afterward; and a person should draw from this an inference for many similar matters that people are accustomed to in that place.

clarification.explanation: A guest given a cup of sugar-water (berachah 'shehakol') and afterward coffee (also 'shehakol') does not bless on the coffee, since it is discharged by the first berachah; and it is good for the guest to intend, with the first drink, to discharge also what will be handed to him afterward.
takeaways: Drinks sharing the same berachah served one after another to a guest — the first discharges those that follow.

paragraphs: If he took something whose berachah is 'borei pri ha'adamah' (Creator of the fruit of the ground) and thought it was a fruit of a tree, and began blessing with the tree-berachah in mind, saying 'Barukh atah Hashem Eloheinu melekh ha'olam' intending to say '...borei pri ha'etz,' but then remembered and concluded 'borei pri ha'adamah' — he has fulfilled his obligation. The same law applies if he took something whose berachah is 'shehakol' and thought it was a tree-fruit, and began blessing intending to say '...ha'etz,' but then remembered and said 'shehakol' — he has fulfilled his obligation. Likewise, if he took a cup of a drink whose berachah is 'shehakol' and thought it was wine as well — the law is the same, that he has fulfilled his obligation. But according to the Rambam, of blessed memory, he has not fulfilled his obligation, since at the essential moment of the berachah his intent was to say something improper. What should he do? Because of the doubt about berachot, he should taste what is in his hand that he blessed over, so that his berachah not be in vain according to all opinions; and because of the Rambam's concern, he should give it to others to bless over and eat, with intent to discharge him, and then he may eat as he wishes. However, if the fruit in his hand was one whose berachah is 'borei pri ha'etz' and he thought it was a ground-fruit, and said 'Barukh atah Hashem Eloheinu melekh ha'olam' intending to say 'borei pri ha'adamah,' but then remembered and concluded 'borei pri ha'etz' — he has fulfilled his obligation according to all opinions, and there is no need to remedy this, since if one blesses 'borei pri ha'adamah' over something whose berachah is 'ha'etz,' he has fulfilled his obligation [in any case]. The same law applies if this was the berachah of 'ha'etz' or of 'borei pri hagafen' and he thought its berachah was 'shehakol,' and he began saying 'shehakol' but concluded with its essential berachah — he has fulfilled his obligation according to all opinions, because if one blesses 'shehakol' over anything, he has fulfilled his obligation.

clarification.explanation: One who took something whose berachah is 'borei pri ha'adamah,' thinking it was a tree-fruit, and began to bless with 'ha'etz' in mind, but then remembered and concluded 'borei pri ha'adamah' — he has fulfilled his obligation. The same applies to a similar mix-up between 'shehakol' and 'ha'etz' or 'wine' — he has fulfilled his obligation (though according to the Rambam one should be stringent, and so it is good to taste it and resolve the doubt by having another person bless and intend to discharge him). But if his true berachah was 'ha'etz' and he thought it was 'ha'adamah,' and he began with 'ha'adamah' but then remembered and concluded 'ha'etz' — he has fulfilled his obligation according to all opinions with no need for remedy, since the berachah 'ha'adamah' is effective even for a tree-fruit.
takeaways: A mix-up between berachah formulas, corrected before finishing, fulfills the obligation in most cases.
'Ha'adamah' over a tree-fruit is effective by the letter of the law; the reverse (ha'etz over ha'adamah) is more doubtful, so it is best to remedy it.

paragraphs: If he blessed over a ground-fruit saying 'borei pri ha'etz,' and immediately, within the time it takes to speak, remembered that he erred and said 'borei pri ha'adamah,' so that his berachah was 'Barukh atah Hashem Eloheinu melekh ha'olam, borei pri ha'etz, borei pri ha'adamah' — he has fulfilled his obligation, even though some disagree, [for] we hold that in a doubt about berachot we are lenient. The same law applies if he erred regarding something whose berachah is 'shehakol' and blessed '[borei pri] ha'etz,' or a drink whose berachah is 'shehakol' and he blessed 'borei pri hagafen.'

clarification.explanation: One who blessed over a ground-fruit 'borei pri ha'etz,' and immediately, within the time it takes to speak, remembered and concluded 'borei pri ha'adamah' (so that the berachah as spoken was '...borei pri ha'etz, borei pri ha'adamah') — he has fulfilled his obligation (even though some disagree, a doubt about berachot is resolved leniently). The same applies to a similar mix-up between 'shehakol' and 'ha'etz' or 'wine'.
takeaways: An immediate correction (within the time it takes to speak) of a mistaken berachah is effective and fulfills the obligation.

paragraphs: One who erred and blessed over bread 'borei minei mezonot' (Creator of various sustenance) has fulfilled his obligation; and even over other kinds of food and drink, if he erred and blessed over them 'borei minei mezonot,' he has fulfilled his obligation, for in the language of the Torah everything is called 'mazon' (sustenance), except for water and salt. Therefore, if he erred and blessed over water 'borei minei mezonot,' he has not fulfilled his obligation, and must say 'Barukh shem kevod malkhuto le'olam va'ed' and go back and bless over the water 'shehakol nihyeh bidvaro,' as mentioned in Chayei Adam, klal 58, se'if 3. And all the laws of errors mentioned above, that one fulfills his obligation after the fact, apply only after the fact; but ideally, before blessing, one must know and have intent for the correct berachah he must recite, so that at the mention of the [divine] Name — which is the essence of the berachah — he will know in truth what he is concluding, and the berachah will be a true one.

clarification.explanation: One who erred and blessed 'borei minei mezonot' over bread, or over other foods and drinks, has fulfilled his obligation, since in the language of the Torah everything is called 'mazon' (sustenance), except for water and salt. Therefore, one who erred and blessed 'minei mezonot' over water has not fulfilled his obligation, and must say 'Barukh shem kevod malkhuto le'olam va'ed' and go back and bless 'shehakol nihyeh bidvaro.' All the laws of error stated above apply only after the fact — but ideally, one must know and intend the correct berachah in advance.
takeaways: 'Borei minei mezonot' after the fact discharges the obligation as a general berachah (except for water and salt) — but ideally one must bless precisely.
